lines.text: A great island settled by sailors from across the ocean, then highland kings, a French colony and a restless republic. This is the story of Madagascar.
Long after Austronesian and African peoples settled the island, the Merina kingdom rose in the highlands, and in time united most of it.
Its royal seat, Antananarivo, grew on the highland hills, and it is still the capital today.
In the eighteenth century King Andrianampoinimerina brought the Merina together under one rule.
Queen Ranavalona the First would reign for over thirty years, banning Christianity and keeping Europe at bay, at a heavy cost in forced labour.
Before her, King Radama the First opened the island to foreign help and brought writing to the Malagasy language.
Ranavalona the Third, born in 1861, would be the last queen of Madagascar.
In 1895 France invaded and conquered the island.
From 1897 Madagascar was a French colony, and the last queen was sent into exile.
Philibert Tsiranana, born in 1912, would become the first president of the free nation.
Didier Ratsiraka, born in 1936, would lead the country for most of the years from 1975 to 2002.
In 1947 the Malagasy rose against French rule, an uprising crushed after two hard years.
In 1960 Madagascar won its independence, an island nation famous for its lemurs.
Andry Rajoelina, born in 1974, would take power in 2009 and later be ousted by the army.
Its wild lands drew new attention, among them the Tsingy de Bemaraha, a forest of razor-sharp limestone needles in the west.
Not far away runs the Avenue of the Baobabs, a dirt road lined with giant trees, one of the island's best-loved sights.
In 2025 young people filled the streets in protest, and the unrest ended in a military takeover.
An island apart, Madagascar is still searching for a steady path of its own.
